svg.text: Criterion B is ruled out for four in five Critically Endangered species.
anyone hoping to reconstruct or audit a Red List assessment
whether this register can say why a species is listed
the species under the threshold have small ranges rather than
area of occupancy against that species' own B2 threshold
one mark per species; rows are categories, not a sequence
multiples of its category's own B2 threshold
Everything right of the rule has a measured area already larger than the
threshold, so criterion B2 cannot be what listed it and the listing rests on
A, C, D or E — none of which a presence-only register can see. Dividing by
each category's own threshold is what lets the three rows share one
boundary: CR's is 10 km², two and a half occupied cells, so almost any
and the ones it could still explain have no data
records held by species under and over their own B2 threshold
records the species holds in the register
Of the 48 Critically Endangered species whose measured area stays under the
threshold, the median record count is one. Their small range is ignorance,
not endemism. Between the two panels there is no Critically Endangered
species here whose listing this register can explain: either the range is
already too large for B2, or there is nothing to measure.
OBIS v3 occurrence/grid precision 5 and checklist/redlist, fetched 2026-09-19. Thresholds from IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria v3.1, second
edition (portals.iucn.org, RL-2001-001-2nd.pdf). B is never satisfied by area alone: it also requires at least two of severe fragmentation or few
locations, continuing decline, and extreme fluctuations — none readable from presence-only data — so this register can rule a species OUT of criterion
B and can never rule one in. occurrence/grid caps at 100,000 features; one species reached it, and since every claim is a lower bound a truncated
count only makes it more conservative.
